newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Golkar takes over 74 percent of vote.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar takes over 74 percent of vote.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar had over 74 percent of the vote with virtually all the general election ballots counted on Saturday, and political analysts said there appeared to have been no significant rise in the protest vote.

Indonesia's Independent Election Monitoring Committee (KIPP), the minority Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the U.S. State Department all criticised the conduct of Thursday's polls, however.
Golkar, assured of victory before a vote was cast, had 74.23 percent of the vote with 88 percent of a possible 125 million votes counted. It won 68 percent in the last elections in 1992.
The PPP -- Golkar's main contender during the most violent election campaign in three decades -- pushed its share up to nearly 23 percent from 17 percent in 1992.

The big loser was the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), badly hit by a leadership battle between ousted party chief Megawati Sukarnoputri and her government-backed replacement, Surjadi.
The PDI saw its share of the votes dive to three percent from 15 percent in 1992. Analysts said both Golkar and the PPP gained at the PDI's expense.
Only 12 percent of the possible votes remained to be counted, but it appeared likely few more would be added to the list. About 90 percent of the electorate voted in 1992.

Analysts doubted there had been any significant rise in the protest vote, known in Indonesia as Golput, or White Group, in which dissidents spoil their ballots or abstain. The Golput vote was put at around three-to-four percent in 1992.
But some analysts said the figure could have been manipulated as a large protest vote would be embarrassing to long-serving President Suharto, who praised the conduct of the election.
"We suspect some manipulation by the government but we cannot prove it," independent analyst Arief Budiman, sometimes referred to as the father of Golput, told Reuters.
"My sources have told me that in some areas the size of Golput was between 15-20 percent," he said.
The lowest turnout was recorded in the capital, Jakarta, where only 69 percent of eligible voters had cast their ballots. Golkar took 57 percent and the PPP 41 percent of the capital's vote.
The PPP has complained of election and voting irregularities and said it would meet next week to decide whether to accept the outcome.

KIPP and the Bangkok-based Asian Forum for Human Rights and Development both issued statements saying glaring irregularities had undermined the credibility of the poll for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives and local and regional assemblies.
The U.S. State Department had called on Friday for changes in Indonesia's political system, saying the elections were strictly controlled by the government.

The worst violence over the elections came in the troubled former Portuguese colony of East Timor, with at least 17 people killed as a result of anti-Indonesian separatist attacks on Wednesday and Thurasday to disrupt the polls.
Despite the violence, 81 percent of the voters turned out, with Golkar getting the lion's share of 84 percent of ballots cast.
Police said on Saturday they had detained 22 suspects in connection with the violence, including 13 "rebels" and nine supporters.
